prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Inside me lived a small donkey. I didn’t believe in magic, but the donkey was a sucker for the stuff. Psychics, illusionists, arthritics who’d predict the rainfall. That was the year I had trouble walking. I over-thought it and couldn’t get the rhythm right. The donkey re-taught me. “This foot. Yes, then that one. And swing your arms as if you’re going to trial to be exonerated of a crime you’ve most definitely committed.” Next, trouble sleeping because I’d need to crank the generator in my chest so frequently. Seeing I was overworked, the donkey finally hauled it out— it looked shiny and new, a silver dollar— and tossed it into a flock of birds who had to fly a long way to find safety. I knew then I was a large and dangerous man, what with this donkey living inside me, but felt futile. One day, during a final lesson on breathing, the donkey asked what kind of jeans I was wearing. I said, “The somber ones.” “Poor kid.” “So will you be staying on for a third year, donkey?” “No. I think I should be leaving soon. I think I should go and await your arrival beside the crumpled river.” “Yes, I suppose you have many important matters to attend to, but maybe one day I will come and join you for a drink or, perhaps, for a brief nap.”

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Inside, Psychics, That

outputs.L1:
Inside me lived a small donkey. I didn’t believe in magic, but the donkey was a sucker for the stuff: psychics, illusionists, arthritics who predicted the rainfall.

That was the year I had trouble walking. I overthought it and couldn’t get the rhythm right. The donkey taught me again. “This foot. Yes, then that one. And swing your arms as if you’re going to trial to be exonerated of a crime you’ve most definitely committed.”

Next came trouble sleeping, because I needed to crank the generator in my chest so frequently. Seeing that I was overworked, the donkey finally hauled it out—it looked shiny and new, like a silver dollar—and tossed it into a flock of birds that had a long way to fly before finding safety.

I knew then that I was a large and dangerous man, what with this donkey living inside me, yet I felt futile.

One day, during a final lesson on breathing, the donkey asked what kind of jeans I was wearing.

“The somber ones,” I said.

“Poor kid.”

“So, will you be staying on for a third year, donkey?”

“No. I think I should be leaving soon. I think I should go and await your arrival beside the crumpled river.”

“Yes, I suppose you have many important matters to attend to. But perhaps one day I will come and join you for a drink—or, perhaps, a brief nap.”

A little burro made its home within me. Sorcery held no appeal for me, though he adored anything supernatural: fortune-tellers, stage magicians, even people whose aching joints foretold rain.

That was the year walking became difficult. I thought so hard about every step that I lost the proper cadence. The burro taught me all over again. “Put down this foot. Good. Now the other. Let your arms sway like you’re headed into court to be cleared of an offense you unquestionably carried out.”

After that, sleep became the problem. The engine in my chest needed constant winding. When the burro noticed my exhaustion, he pulled the mechanism free at last. Bright, pristine, and resembling a silver coin, it was flung among a flock of birds facing a long journey toward refuge.

Then I understood that I was big and perilous—a man with a donkey inside him—yet I still felt powerless.

One day, while giving me a last lesson in how to breathe, the donkey asked which jeans I had on.

“The mournful pair,” I answered.

“You poor child.”

“Will you remain for a third year?”

“No. My departure is near, I think. I ought to wait for you beside the river that lies there all rumpled.”

“Of course. You must have serious business to handle. Still, perhaps someday I’ll meet you there, and we can share a drink—or maybe sleep for a little while.”
outputs.L3:
The narrator imagines that a small donkey lives inside him, a gentle creature that still believes in magic. This inner companion becomes a source of patience and care whenever the narrator’s body fails him. When he struggles to walk, the donkey calmly teaches him again, helping him rediscover the basic rhythm of movement—one, two; one, two—as though walking were something that could be relearned through trust and repetition.

The donkey also eases the narrator’s exhausting struggle to sleep. It removes the endlessly running generator from his chest—the force that keeps his body tense, restless, and awake—and casts it far away. By doing so, the donkey offers him a temporary release from anxiety and physical strain.

Yet the donkey’s presence is not purely comforting. It makes the narrator feel powerful, even dangerous, while at the same time he remains aware of his own futility. He continues to carry a heavy emotional burden, and the strength the donkey gives him cannot entirely overcome his despair.

Eventually, the donkey prepares to leave. It tells the narrator that it will wait beside a “crumpled river,” an image that evokes a mysterious boundary or final resting place. The promised reunion suggests that the donkey will remain connected to him until the end, waiting in a place associated with deep rest, release, or death.
outputs.L4:
The donkey first appeared when my legs began to forget what they were for.

I was standing beside the bed, gripping the wooden post with both hands, while the floor tilted gently away from me. My left foot refused to move. The right trembled in place, burdened by the memory of all the roads it had crossed.

“Too much thinking,” said a voice inside me.

A small gray donkey stood somewhere behind my ribs. His ears brushed the roof of my chest, and his hooves clicked against the hollow places between my breaths.

“What should I do?” I asked.

“Walk,” he replied.

“I’m trying.”

“No. You’re trying not to fall. That is different.”

He showed me how to begin again. First, I was to imagine that my feet were bowls filled to the rim with water. I had to lift each one without spilling. Then he told me the floor was a sleeping animal and must not be startled. Later he ordered me to walk as though I were following a piece of string tied to the moon.

His lessons made no sense, which was precisely why they helped. Sense belonged to the body I had lost—the body that once rose without negotiation, climbed stairs two at a time, and crossed rooms without measuring the distance. The donkey’s instructions belonged to this new country, where every movement required patience and invention.

So I learned to walk again: heel, sole, toe; pause; breathe; begin.

When sleep became difficult, the donkey returned.

At night pain moved through me like a tenant rearranging furniture. I lay awake listening to the house settle, counting the small sounds of darkness. The clock scraped forward. Pipes clicked in the walls. My own heart seemed indecently loud.

“You are lying down badly,” the donkey said.

“I have been lying down all my life.”

“Then you have had plenty of time to learn the wrong way.”

He instructed me to loosen myself one bone at a time. My skull was to become an empty bowl. My shoulders were two sacks of grain lowered from a cart. My spine was a rope left in the rain. Each finger was a tired traveler permitted at last to remove his shoes.

“And what about my thoughts?” I asked.

“Let them graze.”

“Where?”

“Anywhere but here.”

I imagined opening the gate of my mind. My thoughts wandered out—appointments, regrets, names I feared forgetting, things I should have said years earlier. The donkey watched them go without judgment. When the field was empty, he folded his legs beneath him and slept.

I followed.

Months passed. My world narrowed to a handful of rooms, then to the bed, the chair, the window, and the slow corridor between them. Visitors arrived carrying flowers, fruit, and careful expressions. They spoke too brightly. Their eyes traveled over me and quickly away.

The donkey disliked pity.

“It is a poor kind of hay,” he said. “It fills no stomach.”

When breathing grew difficult, he taught me that too.

“Do not drag the air inside,” he said. “Invite it.”

I tried, but each breath snagged somewhere beneath my throat.

“Imagine the air is an old friend.”

“An old friend would know to enter without knocking.”

“Perhaps the door is swollen.”

He made me picture my lungs as two blue rooms with curtains lifting at open windows. He told me to breathe like grass, which sounded impossible until I understood that grass does not chase the wind. It waits and receives.

In. Out.

The smallest tide.

In. Out.

Some days the rooms filled easily. On others, the windows barely opened. The donkey remained beside them, patient and unalarmed.

Finally, he began teaching me how to live.

This seemed strange, since by then everyone understood that I was dying.

“Isn’t it late for that?” I asked.

“It is always late,” he said. “That is why one must begin.”

His last lessons were the simplest. Taste the water. Feel the blanket’s weight. Notice the square of sunlight moving across the wall. Listen when someone speaks, especially if they repeat a story. Let the hand holding yours be enough.

I practiced. A spoonful of soup became weather. Morning light became a country. My sister’s thumb rubbing the back of my hand contained more tenderness than all the words we had avoided.

The donkey grew quieter as I improved.

One evening I found him standing inside me with a little bundle strapped across his back.

“Where are you going?” I asked.

“To the crumpled river.”

I knew the place, although I had never seen it. It lay beyond the last hill of thought, where the land folded in on itself like an old letter. Its water ran slowly between wrinkled banks, carrying leaves, names, and reflections toward a distance no map could hold.

“Why?”

“To wait for you.”

A fear opened in me, cold and immediate.

“Don’t go yet.”

He lowered his head. For the first time, he seemed old. There was silver around his muzzle, and burrs clung to his tail.

“You no longer need me to teach you,” he said.

“I still don’t know how to die.”

“No one does. That is why I will meet you there.”

He walked away through the fields behind my heart. I listened as the sound of his hooves grew softer, then vanished.

Afterward, the room was unchanged. The same curtains stirred. The same glass of water stood beside the bed. Someone had placed fresh flowers on the table, though several petals had already fallen.

I breathed as the donkey had taught me: not pulling, not pleading, only opening the door.

I lay down bone by bone.

I let my thoughts graze.

And when, near dawn, I felt the ground begin to tilt beneath me, I did not struggle against it. I imagined my feet as bowls filled with water. I imagined the earth sleeping under each careful step.

Somewhere ahead, beyond the last hill, a gray donkey was waiting beside a crumpled river.

So I began to walk.

**Inside the World of Psychics**

Inside the mysterious world of psychics, intuition is often described as a bridge between what we know and what we feel. Psychics claim that subtle impressions, emotions, symbols, or visions can reveal information hidden from ordinary perception. Some people consult them for comfort, guidance, or a fresh perspective during uncertain times.

Skeptics argue that psychic readings may rely on observation, suggestion, and broad statements rather than supernatural abilities. Supporters, however, believe that certain individuals possess heightened sensitivity or awareness. Whether viewed as spiritual practice, entertainment, or psychological insight, psychics continue to fascinate people seeking answers beyond the obvious.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short surreal prose poem about a small donkey living inside a person and teaching them how to walk, sleep, and breathe, ending with a bittersweet farewell beside a “crumpled river.”
counterfactuals.output:
A small donkey lived behind my ribs, gray as morning ash. At dawn he tapped my bones and taught me to walk slowly, carrying the invisible without complaint. At night he folded my dreams into straw and showed me how to sleep. When I forgot to breathe, he brayed softly, and my lungs opened like two blue doors.

Years passed. One evening he climbed out through my mouth, old and luminous. I followed him to the edge of a crumpled river.

“Now you know the road,” he said.

I kissed his velvet nose. He crossed alone, while inside me, his little hoofbeats faded into breath.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a flash-fiction piece in the style of contemporary absurdist literary fiction, blending deadpan humor, dream logic, bodily anxiety, and an unexpectedly tender conversation between the narrator and an inner animal.
counterfactuals.output:
At breakfast, I discovered a small deer living behind my left lung.

The doctor showed me the X-ray. There were my ribs, pale as the bars of a ruined gazebo, and there was the deer, curled politely in the dark.

“Is it malignant?” I asked.

The doctor leaned closer. “It looks embarrassed.”

He prescribed salt and told me to avoid sudden weather.

For three weeks I went to work as usual. I answered emails about quarterly objectives while the deer shifted inside me, knocking its antlers against my sternum. Every knock produced a bright little panic.

At night, I dreamed the body had been recalled by the manufacturer. People stood in line at the post office carrying their bodies in damp cardboard boxes. Mine kept leaking through the bottom.

I woke with my hand in my mouth.

“Sorry,” said the deer.

It was the first time it had spoken.

Its voice was not beautiful. It sounded like a man reading train delays through a bad speaker.

“For what?”

“The leaking.”

“That’s me,” I said. “I’ve always done that.”

We were quiet. Somewhere downstairs, a neighbor dropped a spoon and began to cry.

“Are you going to grow?” I asked.

“I don’t know.”

“Will you puncture anything important?”

The deer considered this. “What’s important?”

I listed the heart, the arteries, the stomach, though the stomach had lately behaved more like an enemy nation.

“I’ll be careful,” it said.

After that, we spoke most evenings. I told it about my childhood fear that my knees would reverse themselves. It told me about a meadow it remembered, although it had never been outside my chest.

“In the meadow,” it said, “nothing had a name until it was leaving.”

This annoyed me because it sounded wiser than I was.

One morning, the company announced layoffs. My manager appeared on-screen with the expression of someone whose face had been rented for a funeral. When he said my name, the deer stood up.

My lungs tightened around its legs.

“Please sit down,” I whispered.

“I think we should run.”

“There’s nowhere to run.”

“There never is,” it said. “That’s why it’s called running.”

So I ran.

I ran out of the apartment without shoes, past the bakery, past the school where children were being taught to hide beneath their desks, past the hospital where the doctor stood smoking beneath a NO SMOKING sign. My body lurched and sloshed. Each breath tasted metallic. The deer galloped in place, and for once my heart followed instead of fleeing.

At the river, I stopped.

Across the water, the city continued making copies of itself.

“I’m scared,” I told the deer.

“I know.”

“Are you?”

“Yes.”

This comforted me more than courage would have.

We stood there together, one of us inside the other, both trembling for separate reasons.

Then the deer lowered its head against my heart.

Not to pierce it.

Just to listen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write approximately 250 words of magical realism in which a skeptical narrator discovers a donkey inside himself. Include psychics, difficulty walking, a chest generator, migrating birds, somber jeans, and the suggestion of death without stating it directly.
counterfactuals.output:
I never believed the psychics on Calle Nieve. They sat beneath striped awnings, reading smoke, buttons, the bruises on fruit. When they told me an animal was living inside me, I laughed and paid them nothing.

Then walking became difficult.

At first, my knees merely resisted corners. Soon I could not pass a patch of clover without stopping. Stairs filled me with dread. At night, something shifted behind my ribs and struck my heart with a small, impatient hoof.

The doctor listened through his silver instrument.

“You have a chest generator,” he said.

He showed me the X-ray. Where my lungs should have been stood a gray donkey, its long face lowered, its ears brushing my collarbones. A belt ran from its hind legs to my heart. Each step it took lit a pale bulb somewhere in my blood.

“Nonsense,” I said.

The donkey brayed, and the doctor’s windows trembled.

I bought somber jeans with room in the hips and began leaving bowls of water beside my bed. Migrating birds followed me through the city, arranging themselves above my head in the shape of an arrow. The psychics bowed as I passed.

By autumn, the donkey had grown tired. I could feel it kneeling inside me, folding its thin legs beneath the generator. Streetlamps flickered when I breathed. My shadow no longer reached the end of the block.

Tonight the birds are circling south. I have opened every window, though snow is entering the apartment. Something within me is chewing the last sweet mouthful of clover.

I still do not believe in psychics.

But I have left the door unlocked.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a strange, poetic monologue about illness and mortality, personifying the speaker’s failing body as a wise but eccentric donkey. Make the imagery comic, unsettling, and emotionally poignant.
counterfactuals.output:
My body has become a donkey.

Not a picturesque donkey, mind you, not the sort painted beside a blue-robed saint, nibbling meekly at Bethlehem straw. Mine is a gray, eccentric animal with one eyebrow higher than the other and the bedside manner of a retired executioner.

Every morning he stands inside me and refuses the hill.

“No,” he says, locking his knees.

But we have always gone up the hill, I tell him. There is coffee at the top. There are letters to answer, socks to locate, tiny bureaucracies of being alive.

He shows me his ancient yellow teeth.

“Today,” he says, “we study gravity.”

So down I go—into the chair, into the sheets, into the long arithmetic of symptoms. The doctors knock on his ribs as though choosing a melon. They listen at the doors of his lungs. They consult maps, almanacs, the migratory habits of blood.

My donkey endures this with philosophical contempt.

Once, during an examination, he sneezed inside my heart. The nurse dropped her pen. Somewhere, I believe, a small bell rang beneath the earth.

He is failing, this animal. His hooves are chipped cups. His breath comes in paper bags. His liver wears a hat made of rain. Yet he is wiser than I am and will not be hurried into terror.

At night, when the room fills with the blue aquarium-light of machines, I ask him, Are we dying?

He chews the question sideways.

“We have been dying,” he says, “since they slapped your bottom and you objected.”

This seems rude, but accurate.

Then he tells me death is not a wolf, as I had imagined, nor a tall accountant, nor even the black elevator with its single button. Death, he says, is a field where the fence has fallen. It is thistles. It is moonlight on an empty bucket. It is being relieved, at last, of the obligation to carry someone who keeps calling you *my body* as if you were luggage.

I begin to cry.

The donkey pretends not to notice. He is courteous that way. He noses through my memories instead: my mother singing while burning the soup; the red scarf of a woman who did not love me long enough; my child asleep with one foot outside the blanket, boldly testing eternity.

He lays these things in a row like strange vegetables at a market.

“Look,” he says. “You were fed.”

And because he is a donkey, he eats the scarf.

Because he is my body, I taste wool.

Soon he will lie down. I know this. No carrot, hymn, or clever specialist will persuade him otherwise. His long ears already tilt toward a music I cannot hear.

Still, each morning, I put my arms around his ridiculous neck.

Come on, old philosopher, I whisper. One more hill.

He sighs so deeply the windows tremble. He complains. He farts like a cracked tuba. He calls hope an overrated root vegetable.

Then, with immense reluctance and unbearable tenderness, he takes one step.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me an experimental prose poem narrated by a “large and dangerous man” whose internal donkey retrains his basic bodily functions. Use playful non sequiturs, vivid metaphors, dialogue, and an ambiguous ending involving a river, a drink, and a nap.
counterfactuals.output:
I am a large and dangerous man. Doors reconsider their hinges when I approach. Dogs consult their lawyers. Once, in a bakery, a croissant fainted.

Inside me lives a donkey named Tuesday.

Tuesday was hired to retrain my basic functions.

“Breathing,” he said, kicking one lung like a stubborn accordion, “is not the same as swallowing weather.”

I had always inhaled thunderstorms whole. No wonder my ribs were full of wet umbrellas.

He taught my heart to walk instead of gallop. Clip. Clop. Clip. Clop. Now my pulse arrives wearing little gray shoes, carrying salt in its pockets.

“Again,” Tuesday says.

I blink.

“Too theatrical.”

I blink smaller.

“Again.”

My eyelids descend like two tired guillotines.

Tuesday has opinions about everything. Digestion should be handled alphabetically. Sneezes must apply for permits. The bladder, he insists, is a moon with poor boundaries.

“You cannot threaten gravity,” he tells me.

“I can threaten anything.”

“Then threaten it politely.”

So I stand in the marketplace, vast as a courthouse fire, and whisper to gravity: Please release my knees. Nearby, a cabbage rings a silver bell. Nobody claims responsibility.

For years I ate like a collapsing empire. I slept with both fists loaded. I woke chewing the furniture of my dreams. Tuesday changed all that. He harnessed my hunger to a blue cart and made it haul turnips through the corridors of my abdomen.

“Slowly,” he said. “A body is not a war just because it has borders.”

This offended me.

Then it saved my life.

Or perhaps it only made my life easier to misplace.

This morning Tuesday retrained thirst. He led me down through the red machinery, past the liver’s dim tavern, past the kidneys counting their transparent coins.

At the bottom of me, a river was waiting.

It smelled of iron, mint, and someplace I had once been gentle.

“Drink,” said Tuesday.

“From myself?”

“From wherever you think this is.”

I knelt. The river widened—or I became smaller. My dangerous hands floated away like two overturned boats. Somewhere, a croissant regained consciousness.

I drank.

Tuesday drank.

The river drank us back.

Afterward, on the bank—or in the glass, or under my own tongue—we lay down for a nap.

“Will we wake?” I asked.

The donkey closed one enormous eye.

The water kept answering, but not in words.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
